title: What law is (ST I-II.90.4)
hookLine: an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community

lines: WHAT MAKES A RULE A LAW?
cards: A red light, very late at night. No cars in any direction, no camera, nobody on the sidewalk. The light stays red, and a driver sits there anyway, drumming on the wheel, feeling slightly ridiculous.
Or because the rule is actually for something? Thomas Aquinas wanted to know what makes a rule a law at all, and not just somebody's order with a penalty attached.
He packed his answer into one sentence, and that sentence is today.

teach.b: Here's the sentence, in plain English. Law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community, and made known. A piece at a time.
First, reason. A law isn't just a strong will. If a ruler's command isn't measured by reason, Thomas says, it's closer to wrongdoing than to law.
A law points actions toward an end.
Second, the common good: the good of the whole community, not one person's advantage, not even the lawmaker's.

teach.h: BY THE ONE WHO CARES FOR THE COMMUNITY.
teach.b: Third, the one who has care of the community. Making law belongs to the whole people, or to someone who stands in for them and looks after them.
Fourth, it has to be made known. A law nobody could ever learn binds nobody. And that piece has a lovely turn: the deepest law, the natural law, was made known when God placed it in human minds.
Now the edge of the sentence. If a rule serves the ruler against the people, Thomas says it's more like violence than law.
He doesn't say every such rule may be ignored on the spot; sometimes it's wiser to bear it than to cause greater harm. But it isn't law in the full sense.
In Proverbs, in the Douay-Rheims, wisdom speaks: "By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things." So for Thomas, law isn't the enemy of freedom.
A good law is reason, handed to a community, so people can live well together.

how: Catholic social teaching draws on Thomas's account of law and the common good, and the Catechism teaches that authority is legitimate when it seeks the common good by morally acceptable means.

o: any command backed by a strong penalty
whatever most people vote to require
a rule of reason made for the common good

games.q: Thomas's sentence on law — tap the pairs.
p: the one who cares for the community

s: for Thomas, a law is whatever the ruler wants
a command not measured by reason, he says, is closer to wrongdoing than to law.
Thomas says a law must be made known
a law nobody could learn binds nobody. the natural law was made known in human minds.
Thomas says any unfair rule may be ignored on the spot
he calls such rules more like violence than law, but says it's sometimes wiser to bear them than to cause greater harm.

games.q: a ruler issues a rule that helps only himself and hurts his people. is it a law, by Thomas's sentence?
o: yes: whatever a ruler commands is law.
not in the full sense: it's more like violence.
yes, as long as it was announced.
games.why: Thomas says a rule against the common good is more like violence than law, though bearing it is sometimes wiser than causing greater harm.

practice: Bring to mind a rule you follow most days without thinking, a speed limit, a house rule, a line at the coffee shop, and run it through Thomas's sentence: is it reasonable, whose good does it serve, who made it, how did you learn it?
If it passes, notice what it protects, someone's safety, someone's time, a little peace, and let your keeping of it be glad rather than grudging.

wordCard.voice: What law is. For Thomas, an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community, and made known. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: law.

carryVoice: Your line: reason for the common good. A good rule is a small gift to the people it protects. Rest well.
